note: Documented cases found by web search on 22 October 2026. Each claim is what the cited source reports. Where sources disagree, the case says so. A record may cite a case from this pool only; any other claim must be written as an inference from the model's principle.

cases.case: Private equity acquisition of US hospitals, JAMA study
cases.claim: A JAMA study by Kannan, Bruch and Song (2023) compared 51 US hospitals acquired by private equity with 259 matched control hospitals, using Medicare claims for 2009 to 2019. Hospital-acquired conditions rose by about 25 per cent relative to the controls, most of the rise coming from falls and central-line bloodstream infections. Surgical-site infection rates reached about twice their earlier level, while surgical volume fell by about 8 per cent. Thirty-day mortality after discharge did not change, and in-hospital deaths edged down slightly.
cases.source: Kannan, Bruch and Song, JAMA (2023), DOI 10.1001/jama.2023.23147, as summarised by AHRQ PSNet
cases.caveat: These comparisons are observational. The acquired hospitals' patients were younger, included fewer dual-eligible patients and were more often transferred out, so the patient mix changed as well. The paper itself was not read; these figures come from summaries.

cases.case: Emergency department deaths at private equity hospitals, Annals study
cases.years: Study year not stated in the search results
cases.claim: A study in the Annals of Internal Medicine reported that emergency department death rates at private equity-acquired hospitals were about 13 per cent higher than at comparable hospitals. A researcher quoted in the coverage named reduced staffing as the most likely cause.
cases.source: Annals of Internal Medicine study on private equity and emergency departments, as reported by NBC Boston (secondary)
cases.caveat: Known only from news coverage. The study design and its comparison group were not checked. The staffing cause is the view of a researcher quoted in the coverage, not a finding reported by the study.

cases.case: For-profit and non-profit hospital mortality, a 2002 meta-analysis
cases.claim: A 2002 systematic review and meta-analysis in CMAJ compared mortality at private for-profit and private non-profit hospitals. After adjustment for confounders, the adult estimate was a relative risk of death of about 1.02 for for-profit hospitals (95 per cent confidence interval roughly 1.003 to 1.038). The perinatal estimate, drawn from one study, was about 1.095.
cases.source: CMAJ systematic review and meta-analysis of for-profit and non-profit hospital mortality (2002, 166(11): 1399 to 1406)
cases.caveat: The studies are observational and highly variable, and the underlying US data cover 1982 to 1995. The review measures mortality only. The search found no newer or contrary meta-analysis.

cases.claim: Chancellor Nicolas Rolin and his wife Guigone de Salins founded the Hospices de Beaune in 1443 as a poor-relief hospital, at a time when raiders, famine and plague had impoverished the town. Its income came from salt works and wine sales. Sources date the formal founding to 4 August 1443 and admissions to 1 January 1452.
cases.source: France Today, Hospices de Beaune: The Remarkable Story of Burgundy's Palace of the Poor (secondary)
cases.caveat: The dates come from secondary sources. The search did not give the date when the hospital's own care ended, and one source gives two different dates for it.

cases.case: Kaiser Permanente's prepaid group practice, from 1933
cases.claim: Sidney Garfield began a prepaid group practice in 1933 at a Mojave Desert hospital that served workers on the Colorado River Aqueduct. Workers paid about five cents a day through a prepayment arrangement. Garfield and Henry J. Kaiser co-founded Kaiser Permanente, which the company's own history dates to 1945.
cases.source: Kaiser Permanente, Sidney Garfield, pioneer of modern health care (company history)
cases.caveat: Sources differ on the bed count of the first hospital. The search gave no membership figure for 1945.

cases.case: State ownership of health facilities in the Soviet Union, from 1918
cases.claim: A July 1918 decree put health facilities under state ownership and declared care free to everyone. A PubMed Central review describes underfunding and a heavy reliance on inpatient care in the system that followed.
cases.source: PubMed Central article PMC6220729 on the Soviet health system (secondary)
cases.caveat: Another paper dates the start of implementation to the late 1920s. The review's description of the system is a summary, not a measured outcome.
